newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Delight as UK grants passports to HK minorities.
newsitem.headline: Delight as UK grants passports to HK minorities.

text.p: Hong Kong's ethnic minorities welcomed Britain's change of heart in granting them passports, a move that allays fears they may face statelessness after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
"I'm absolutely delighted as you can no doubt imagine. It is the news that we have been waiting for many, many years," said Ravi Gidumal, director of the Indian Resources Group.
The Council of Hongkong Indian Associations also welcomed the British decision, announced late on Tuesday.
"Through all this, we have kept our faith in the traditional British sense of fairness and I am glad to see that our faith was not misplaced," chairman Kewalram Sital said in a statement.
"The British sense of justice has prevailed against all odds and the ethnic minorities of Hong Kong are about to receive what is their due," Sital said.

The decision affects an estimated 5,000-8,000 people, most of them of Indian and Pakistani descent whose families have lived in Hong Kong for generations and who are entitled to British travel documents but not the right to settle in Britain.
They will have residency rights in Hong Kong after the handover but it remains unclear whether they will be entitled to Chinese nationality.

The British announcement came after a China-appointed panel decided last Saturday to dilute Hong Kong's civil liberties laws, spreading anger and despondency ahead of the transition at midnight on June 30, 1997.
The United States Consul-General in Hong Kong, Richard Boucher, said on Wednesday the Chinese decision threatened to erode international confidence in post-1997 Hong Kong.

"Over time we have been reassured that the thing that would change is the Governor and the flag... But yet we keep seeing repeated serious steps where politicial actions are taken with, frankly, little regard of Hong Kong laws and the Hong Kong people," Boucher said on Hong Kong radio.

China promised in a 1984 Sino-British treaty governing the handover of Hong Kong to China to maintain freedoms and Hong Kong's capitalist way of life intact for 50 years under a policy it calls "one country, two systems".
China insists the plans will have no material effect on freedoms and civil liberties in Hong Kong.
"When we see repeated actions taken that have to be explained, it gets more difficult to think that things will indeed stay the way they are," Boucher said. "That's bad news."

Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, has defended the proposals, arguing that the international community does not fully understand the situation in Hong Kong and that the changes will not dilute civil liberties.

"There are negative impacts because many news reports are negative and misleading. I think we need to spend more time to explain to them. Gradually, they will understand," Tung told reporters on Tuesday.
